Note::split_chars¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

TokenBatch Note::split_chars() const

Split Every Text Cell Into Unicode Scalars¶

split_chars() tokenizes each Text lane into its decoded Unicode scalar values. It is useful when an algorithm needs code-point-level traversal while retaining the boundary of every original cell. The result is a TokenBatch: all scalar strings are concatenated in tokens(), and Int64 offsets() map each flattened source lane to its half-open token range.

This is deliberately not a byte splitter and not a user-perceived character or grapheme splitter. A multibyte UTF-8 scalar such as é or 🙂 becomes one token, while a decomposed e followed by a combining acute accent becomes two tokens. Use lengths_graphemes() when cursor positions or visible character counts require grapheme-cluster semantics.

For a source with N = numel() lanes, offsets() has N + 1 entries. Source lane i owns tokens() positions [offsets[i], offsets[i + 1]). Empty source lanes contribute no tokens, so adjacent offsets may be equal. Higher-rank inputs are traversed in flat row-major order; the TokenBatch retains lane boundaries rather than the source rank because each lane may produce a different number of scalars.

Only Text Notes are accepted. Bytes are not implicitly decoded, and Bool, Int64, and Float64 are not formatted into text. Convert deliberately before calling when that is the desired operation. An undefined receiver propagates as an undefined token Note with the canonical offset Note [0].

The operation is non-mutating. It walks the UTF-8 sequence widths already held by the Text Note, allocates one small Text cell per scalar plus the offsets Note, and is linear in source bytes. It is not the malformed-input validation boundary; use to_utf8_strict() before splitting when text originates from an untrusted byte source. Large Notes are processed by the batched tokenization path, but output cardinality still determines allocation cost.

Example 1: ASCII And Multibyte Scalars¶

const auto batch = pluss::note::make({"Aé🙂", "Hi"}).split_chars();

std::cout << "tokens=" << batch.tokens() << '\n';
std::cout << "offsets=[";
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < batch.offsets().integers().size(); ++i)
  std::cout << (i ? ", " : "") << batch.offsets().integers()[i];
std::cout << "]\n";

Output¶

tokens=Note(shape=[5], dim=1, numel=5, encoding=utf8)
["A", "é", "🙂", "H", "i"]
offsets=[0, 3, 5]

The first source cell owns three tokens and the second owns two, despite the different UTF-8 byte widths involved.

Example 2: Recover Each Source Lane¶

const auto batch = pluss::note::make({"Aé🙂", "Hi"}).split_chars();
for (std::int64_t row = 0; row < 2; ++row) {
  std::cout << "row " << row << ": [";
  for (auto i = batch.offsets().integers()[row];
       i < batch.offsets().integers()[row + 1]; ++i) {
    std::cout << (i == batch.offsets().integers()[row] ? "\"" : ", \"")
              << batch.tokens().at(i) << '"';
  }
  std::cout << "]\n";
}

Output¶

row 0: ["A", "é", "🙂"]
row 1: ["H", "i"]

Example 3: Combining Marks Remain Separate Scalars¶

const auto batch = pluss::note::make("e\u0301").split_chars();
std::cout << "decomposed token-count=" << batch.tokens().numel()
          << " byte-lengths=" << batch.tokens().at(0).size()
          << ',' << batch.tokens().at(1).size() << '\n';

Output¶

decomposed token-count=2 byte-lengths=1,2

The two scalars may render as one visual glyph. Normalize first if canonical composition is part of the intended pipeline.

Example 4: Matrices Flatten Into Ragged Rows¶

const auto grid = pluss::note::make(
    std::vector<std::string>{"ab", "", "x", "YZ"},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 2>{2, 2});
const auto batch = grid.split_chars();

std::cout << "grid source-shape=[" << grid.size(0) << ", " << grid.size(1)
          << "] offsets=";
for (const auto offset : batch.offsets().integers()) std::cout << offset << ' ';
std::cout << '\n';

Output¶

grid source-shape=[2, 2] offsets=0 2 2 3 5

The empty cell is the second flattened lane and therefore contributes the repeated boundary 2, 2.

Example 5: Undefined Propagates Structurally¶

const auto batch = pluss::Note::undefined().split_chars();
std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << "undefined batch=" << batch.defined()
          << " tokens-defined=" << batch.tokens().defined()
          << " offset=" << batch.offsets().int_item() << '\n';

Output¶

undefined batch=true tokens-defined=false offset=0

The batch object is valid and its offsets are canonical, while token absence remains observable.

Example 6: Non-Text Dtypes Reject¶

try {
  (void)pluss::note::bytes(std::vector<std::string>{"abc"}).split_chars();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "Bytes split: rejected\n";
}
try {
  (void)pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{1, 2}).split_chars();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "Int64 split: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

Bytes split: rejected
Int64 split: rejected
